title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Economics Second Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In First Term you learned the basic ideas of economics. In Second Term you will apply them to Nigeria. You will study how the Nigerian economy is built, what each part of the country produces, how we farm and mine, how banks and other financial institutions work, what money is and why we use it, how goods travel from the factory to your home, how businesses raise money, and how a country chooses between producing different goods.

The notes are written in simple words with tables and diagrams. Read each unit slowly and try the practice questions at the end. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: The Nigerian Economy and the Structure of Industry
summary: Nigeria's mixed economy, its size and exports, and the three groups of industry: primary, secondary and tertiary.

p: Nigeria has a mixed economy. Private businesses own most of the economic activity, but the government regulates some sectors and controls others (for example, parts of oil and gas, power and railways). Private businesses try to earn profit, so the economy is capitalist at its core.

Nigeria has over 200 million people, which makes it one of the most populous countries in the world and the largest in Africa. A large population gives a large labour force and a large market for goods.

Nigeria depends heavily on exports and imports. Petroleum is the biggest export, and Nigeria is one of the largest oil exporters in Africa. In recent years, about 90 per cent of Nigeria's export earnings have come from petroleum and gas. Most of its crude oil is bought by countries such as India, Spain, the Netherlands and the United States. Relying on one product is risky, because a fall in oil prices reduces the country's income.
Industries are grouped by what they do with resources.

What it does

sections.h: How the three industries work together
p: Think of a loaf of bread. The farmer (primary) grows wheat. The flour mill and bakery (secondary) turn it into bread. The shop owner and the delivery rider (tertiary) bring the bread to you. If any group stops working, the others suffer.

The secondary sector has great power to change an economy because it adds value to raw materials, gives skilled jobs and creates goods for export. The tertiary sector is now the largest sector of the world economy by value, and in Nigeria it is also the biggest part of the economy.
Besides oil, Nigeria exports agricultural products such as cocoa, rubber, sesame seeds, cashew nuts and palm products. Palm oil was Nigeria's most important export before oil was found.

title: Economic Activities of the Six Geopolitical Zones
summary: The states in each of Nigeria's six zones and the main things people do and produce there.

p: Nigeria is divided into six geopolitical zones: North-West, North-East, North-Central, South-West, South-East and South-South. The land, climate and resources are different in each zone, so people do different kinds of work. This is an example of geographical specialisation, which you studied in First Term.

title: Agriculture: Meaning, Components and Systems
summary: What agriculture is, its four parts (crops, livestock, fishing, forestry), food crops and cash crops, and the four farming systems.

p: Agriculture is the production of crops, animals, fish and forest resources for food and other uses by people. It is the main job of a very large share of people in West Africa.

Crop production: growing crops. Food crops are grown mainly to be eaten at home, such as maize, rice, beans, cocoyam, yam, tomatoes, millet. Cash crops are grown mainly to be sold at home or abroad, such as cocoa, oil palm, rubber, palm kernel, cotton and groundnut. A crop can be both: a farmer may eat some of his maize and sell the rest.
Livestock: rearing domestic animals such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, horses and donkeys, and also poultry. Most are reared for meat, milk, eggs, hides and work.
Fishing: catching and breeding fish from rivers, lakes, ponds and the sea. It is a main job in riverine and coastal areas.
Forestry: looking after economic trees and taking products from forests such as timber, plywood, poles, paper pulp and boats.

Plantation farming: large estates of land permanently planted with one commercial crop, such as rubber, oil palm, sugarcane or cotton. The land may belong to government, private people or companies. It needs a lot of capital and many workers.

Peasant (subsistence) farming: farming on small pieces of land, mostly by family labour, with simple tools such as cutlasses, hoes and axes. Much of the produce is eaten by the family and only the surplus is sold. Land is often owned by the family or community.
Co-operative farming: farmers form a society or union to help one another. Together they obtain loans, buy fertiliser and seeds, hire or buy machines and sell their produce at better prices.

Mechanized farming: using machines such as tractors, ploughs and harvesters instead of human labour. It allows large-scale production, but machines are costly and the system is not yet widespread in West Africa.

title: Importance and Problems of Agriculture, and How Nigerian Farming Has Changed
summary: Why agriculture matters, the problems farmers face and their solutions, and the story of Nigerian agriculture since oil was found.

p: It gives raw materials to industries (cotton for textiles, cocoa for chocolate, rubber for tyres). It gives food. It gives jobs to many people. It creates a market for industrial products such as tools, fertiliser and clothes. It is a source of income for farmers and of foreign exchange for the country. It supplies labour to industries when people move from farms to towns.

Illiteracy and ignorance of modern methods. Lack of medical facilities in rural areas. Use of crude tools such as hoes and cutlasses. Poverty of farmers. Lack of credit (loans). Poor storage, so food rots. Poor roads and transport. Problems of the land tenure system (land is divided among families or owned by a few, so farms are small). Pests and diseases. Natural disasters such as flood and drought.

Give farmers cheap loans. Build better roads and storage. Discourage the movement of young people from rural areas to towns (by providing amenities there). Encourage the use of machines. Control pests and diseases. Provide medical facilities. Educate farmers. Use research to produce improved seeds and animals. Use irrigation so that farming does not depend only on rain.

Before the 1970s, Nigeria exported cocoa, palm oil, groundnut and cotton. When oil prices rose sharply in the 1970s, money from petroleum became the main source of income. Many young people left the villages for the towns, and farm production fell. By the mid-1970s Nigeria had to import food such as rice. Population also grew fast, so the food shortage became worse.

Many farmers are small-scale, using hoes and cutlasses on small plots. Poor storage, poor transport, lack of money and the shortage of land hold farm output down. Yam and cassava are the main food crops in the south. Sorghum, millet, cowpea (beans) and maize are the main food crops in the north. Rice is grown in many areas. Oil palm, cocoa and rubber are the main industrial crops of the south, and groundnut and cotton of the north. Cocoa is still the biggest agricultural export.

Governments have tried to help. The Operation Feed the Nation programme (1976 to 1980) encouraged people to farm any empty plot of land. In the 1980s the government closed the produce marketing boards, which had paid farmers prices fixed by government, so that farmers could be paid better prices and plant more tree crops. Governments also set up plantations of oil palm, rubber and cocoa. Fulani herders are still the main source of beef, and fishing supplies more than half of the fish eaten in the country. Lake Chad, the coastal waters and the rivers are the main sources of fish.

title: Mining: Meaning, Components, Minerals and Their Uses
summary: What mining is, the three parts of the mining sector, Nigerian minerals and where they are found, and what they are used for.

p: Mining is taking useful minerals and metals out of the earth, including from under the sea. Examples are crude oil, gold, iron ore, diamond, coal, limestone, copper and gravel. Crude oil was first found in commercial quantity at Oloibiri (now in Bayelsa State) in 1956 and became the most important source of government money and foreign exchange. Coal mining began near Enugu in 1915.
The mining sector is all the businesses that look for mineral deposits and take valuable minerals from the earth to sell. It has three components.
1. Exploration and mining (upstream): finding mineral deposits in amounts large enough to be worth mining, and then digging them out.

2. Processing and beneficiation (midstream): changing minerals from their natural form into finished or semi-finished goods. For example, cement companies turn limestone into cement, and a jeweller turns raw gold into rings and watches.
3. Marketing and transportation: wholesalers, retailers, agents and drivers who move the products to the final users.

title: Effects of Mining and How to Reduce the Bad Effects
summary: The good and bad effects of mining on a country and its people, and the steps that can reduce harm.

p: Revenue: taxes, royalties and licence fees from mining companies give money to government. Raw materials: limestone for cement, granite and gravel for building. Better living standards: money from minerals can pay for roads, schools, hospitals and power. Foreign exchange: exports of oil, coal and tin earn dollars and other foreign money and can improve the balance of payments (the record of a country's payments to other countries and receipts from them in a year). Employment: mining gives jobs in digging, processing, transport and sales.

Deforestation: large areas of forest are cleared for mines. Food chain damage: mining chemicals and heavy metals enter water and soil, poison plants and fish and finally harm people who eat them. Air pollution: heavy machines and burning gas release harmful gases and dust. Erosion: digging deep pits makes land unfit for farming and houses. Noise: loud machines can damage the hearing of workers who have no ear protection. In oil areas such as the Niger Delta, oil spills also destroy farms and fishing waters.

sections.h: Ways to reduce the bad effects
p: Government rules: laws that make companies mine responsibly, protect workers and clean up after mining. Reduce consumption: when we buy the newest phone or clothes we do not need, factories use more minerals. Using things longer reduces demand. Education: teach children and the public about the harm mining can do. Proper waste disposal: companies should treat and recycle waste. Better efficiency: watching the supply chain closely helps to find where waste can be cut, so mining harms the environment less. Replanting trees and restoring mined land also helps.

title: Financial Institutions and Their Types
summary: What a financial institution is, and the traditional institutions, insurance companies, the central bank, commercial banks, development banks and the stock exchange.

p: Financial institutions are organisations that deal mainly in money. They collect savings and spare money from individuals and firms and lend it to those who need it for spending or investment. They link savers with borrowers.

The esusu (also called ajo or adashi in different areas) is a traditional savings club. Members agree to pay a fixed sum at regular times, and each time one member collects the whole amount, until everyone has received a turn. It is a way of saving and borrowing without a bank.

An insurance company protects a person or business against loss. The customer pays a small amount, called a premium, and the company pays when the loss it has agreed to cover (fire, theft, accident, death) happens. Insurance companies also invest the premiums they collect.

The central bank manages the country's money and banking system. Its functions are to issue notes and coins; to act as the bankers' bank (commercial banks keep accounts with it); to act as banker and adviser to the government; to act as lender of last resort (commercial banks borrow from it when no one else will lend); to control the supply of money and credit; and to look after the foreign reserves.

Commercial banks accept deposits from customers and pay them back on demand. Their functions are to accept deposits (current, savings and fixed deposit accounts); to lend money to individuals, businesses and government; to keep valuables safely; to make payments and transfers for customers (cheques, transfers, cards); and to help government to circulate new money and withdraw old money. Examples: Access Bank, GTBank, Zenith Bank, First Bank, UBA.

Development banks are set up by government to give long-term loans at low interest to special sectors such as agriculture, industry and housing that ordinary banks may not want to lend to. Examples in Nigeria are the Bank of Industry (BOI), the Bank of Agriculture (BOA) and the Federal Mortgage Bank. (Older notes mention NIDB, NBCI and NACB. These were merged into newer banks such as the Bank of Industry.)
The stock exchange is a market that brings together people who want to sell shares and stocks and people who want to buy them. In Nigeria it is now called the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) in Lagos.

title: The Money Market, the Capital Market and Other Institutions
summary: Short-term and long-term markets for money, primary and secondary markets, and special terms such as bureau de change, debenture and market capitalisation.

p: The money market is where short-term funds (usually one year or less) are lent and borrowed. It helps those with too little money (the deficit sector) to borrow from those with extra money (the surplus sector). The institutions in it are commercial banks, merchant banks, the Central Bank, discount houses and hire purchase companies. Its benefits: the public can invest money for a short time and earn interest, and firms and governments can borrow quickly for short-term projects.

The capital market is the market for long-term funds (more than one year) used for investment. The Nigerian Exchange is its centre. The capital market has two divisions. The primary market sells new securities (new shares and debentures) for the first time. Ways of offering include offer for subscription (inviting the public to buy), rights issue and debentures. The secondary market is the stock exchange, where securities that were already issued are bought and sold between investors. Institutions that work in this market include insurance companies, issuing houses, development banks, investment banks, mortgage banks and the stock exchange.

head: Money market
Capital market
rows: Treasury bills, bank loans, commercial paper

p: Bureau de change: a licensed business that buys and sells foreign money (for example dollars and pounds). They were authorised in 1989 to make foreign exchange easier to get for small users.
Discount house: a special non-bank institution that collects money from the surplus sector and channels it to the deficit sector. It acts between the CBN, banks and other institutions.
Distressed banks: banks with problems such as shortage of cash, poor earnings and loans that are not repaid.
New issues: shares or other securities offered to the public for the first time in the primary market.
Rights issue: new shares offered first to the company's existing shareholders in proportion to the shares they hold, usually at a price below the market price.
Debenture: a loan to a company that earns fixed interest.
Preference share: a share whose holders are paid their fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders.
Market capitalisation: the market value of all a company's shares. It equals the price of one share multiplied by the number of shares. Example: 1 million shares at N50 each gives N50 million.
